title: YOU KEEP TELLING THE DEVIL TO FLEE—BUT YOU MAY HAVE SKIPPED THE COMMAND THAT COMES FIRST
paragraphs:
YOU KEEP TELLING THE DEVIL TO FLEE—BUT YOU MAY HAVE SKIPPED THE COMMAND THAT COMES FIRST
“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” is biblical. But when those eight words are pulled away from the sentence surrounding them, we can accidentally turn a call to surrender into a slogan about spiritual power.
There is a Bible verse people love to shout when darkness gets close.
When an old addiction knocks on the door again.
When lust comes back after you promised God it was over.
When bitterness starts replaying the conversation.
When the enemy seems to be attacking your mind, your marriage, your family, your faith.
“RESIST THE DEVIL AND HE WILL FLEE!”
But that is not the whole sentence.
And what comes immediately before those famous words may be the very thing we have been avoiding.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
Because there is an order here.

And perhaps one reason some Christians feel exhausted from constantly fighting darkness is that we have become very interested in resisting the devil while remaining strangely reluctant to surrender completely to God.
But we do not want to surrender the relationship feeding it.
But we keep returning privately to what enslaves us.
We want God to rebuke the darkness around us while asking Him not to touch certain darkness within us.
Then we wonder why the battle feels endless.
The original Greek makes James’ words difficult to soften.
“Ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ θεῷ· ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ, καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.”
Hypotagēte oun tō Theō; antistēte de tō diabolō, kai pheuxetai aph’ hymōn.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
It comes from ὑποτάσσω, hypotassō, carrying the sense of placing oneself under, subjecting oneself, submitting to rightful authority.
And those positions are not contradictory.
The Christian who kneels before Christ is precisely the Christian who can stand against what opposes Christ.
That changes the picture, doesn't it?
Spiritual warfare is not you standing in the middle of your bedroom trying to convince demons that you are powerful.
The Gospel was never about proving how powerful you are.
It is about belonging to the One who is.
The One before whom darkness ultimately has no throne.
But there is something even more uncomfortable hiding in the context of James 4.
James was not speaking to people who merely needed a motivational speech about Satan.
James confronts quarrels, disordered desires, selfish motives, friendship with the world, pride, double-mindedness, sin, and the need for repentance.
“From whence come wars and fightings among you?”
Then he begins exposing what is happening inside them.
That matters because sometimes we blame the devil for things Scripture is asking us to repent of.
Not every angry outburst can be dismissed as “spiritual attack.”
Not every financial disaster is Satan attacking your finances.
Sometimes you need wisdom and self-control.
Not every collapsing relationship is automatically demonic opposition.
Sometimes pride has been sitting at the dinner table for years.
Not every recurring temptation disappears because you verbally rebuke Satan.
Sometimes Jesus is calling you to cut off access, confess sin, seek accountability, flee temptation, renew your mind, and stop protecting the very environment in which that temptation keeps growing.
But personal responsibility is real too.
And James refuses to let us use one truth to escape another.
Maybe that is why this passage hurts before it heals.
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.”
“Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.”
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.”
This is much deeper than shouting at the devil.
And surrender is where many of us begin negotiating.
Except the part I refuse to handle honestly.
Except the room where I keep what they did to me.
And whatever comes after “except” may be exactly where this passage is trying to reach us.
Because there is a difference between wanting Jesus to rescue you from consequences and wanting Jesus to rule you as Lord.
Not because condemnation is the goal.
James himself says only a few verses earlier:
What extraordinary words to find in a passage filled with confrontation.
The purpose of biblical conviction is not to convince you that you are beyond redemption.
It is to bring you out of hiding.
There is a massive difference between condemnation that drives you away from Christ and conviction that drives you toward Christ.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself perfectly so Jesus might finally tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces that sinners who could never save themselves have been offered reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
And grace does not merely forgive the rebel.
Grace begins teaching the rebel to surrender.
Maybe you have been fighting the same hidden battle for months.
Your family thinks you are okay.
People at church see the version of you that knows when to smile.
Your Bible may even have highlighted verses about victory.
The you who promised God, “Never again.”
And somewhere along the way you started wondering whether Jesus had finally become tired of you.
Your sin should never be minimized.
But neither should the mercy of Christ.
The answer is not pretending the chain is harmless.
The answer is bringing the chain into the presence of the One who breaks chains.
Do not rename bondage because repentance hurts.
Do not call lust “just being human” as an excuse to surrender to it.
Do not call pride “knowing my worth.”
Do not call unforgiveness “protecting my peace.”
Far more deeply than we do.
And because He understands what sin destroys, His grace does not simply pat us on the head while we walk toward destruction.
Maybe the most spiritual thing you can do tonight is not scream louder at Satan.
Because surrender means God gets access to the locked rooms.
The version of yourself you constructed so nobody discovers how tired you really are.
But there is something beautiful about finally having nothing left to hide from the One who already sees everything.
You do not surprise Jesus with your wounds.
You do not shock Him with your history.
You do not reveal a secret He somehow missed.
And still the Gospel calls you toward Him.
A woman with a ruined reputation.
A tax collector despised by his community.
A disciple who would deny Him three times.
Jesus never treated sin as harmless.
But neither did He treat repentant sinners as disposable.
That is the scandal of grace.
Grace does not pretend you never sinned.
Grace announces that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Imagine looking toward Jesus after that.
Imagine realizing the Man you swore you would never abandon heard you deny knowing Him.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Yet Peter's story did not end beside that fire.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming people who finally stop running from the truth and run toward Him.
Maybe your greatest spiritual battle right now is not getting Satan to leave the room.
Maybe it is deciding who owns the room.
Who owns the hidden version of you?
Because James does not begin with the devil.
And when you fall, do not turn failure into permission to stay down.
Some battles require more than one dramatic prayer.
Sometimes resisting temptation looks remarkably ordinary.
Opening Scripture when your feelings are screaming something else.
Forgiving again when the memory resurfaces.
Choosing truth when nobody would know if you chose differently.
Sometimes resistance sounds like a trembling person whispering:
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your struggle. Wisdom and appropriate privacy matter. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become another person's reason to believe there is still hope.
Let somebody scrolling through darkness discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescue.
We are people whose hope is in a Rescuer.
And please do not keep this article imprisoned on this page.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
Not because sharing Christian content makes somebody more righteous.
We are saved by the grace of God through faith, not by social-media performance.
Someone may be blaming Satan while protecting compromise.
Someone may be drowning in shame and desperately needs to hear, “He giveth more grace.”
Someone may be one honest prayer away from finally coming out of hiding.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions feel distant tomorrow.
Come back when the battle gets loud.
Come back when you are tempted to negotiate again.
We want this community to be somewhere people encounter daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Not to prove that you love God.
Share because grace was freely given.
Not because an algorithm can save souls.
But a share can put the message of Christ in front of another human being.
And sometimes God uses something as ordinary as one person sharing truth to begin an extraordinary conversation.
And if this convicted you, comment something real.
Maybe tonight is not the night you become stronger at pretending.
Maybe tonight is the night you surrender.
Because the verse you thought was mainly about making the devil run may actually begin with God asking you to come home.
The devil is not the center of James 4.
And ultimately, for the Christian, Jesus is.
You do not defeat darkness by becoming obsessed with darkness.
And you keep following the Savior who carried sinners' shame all the way to a Roman cross, rose from the grave, and still calls broken people out of hiding.
So the next time you hear someone say:
“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you…”
remember the words that come first.
Maybe those are the words we left out because they demand the one thing our pride has always hated giving away.
And perhaps the freedom you have been begging God for begins when you finally stop asking Jesus merely to help run your life…
and surrender your life to Him.
You were never called merely to make the devil flee; you were called to belong completely to Jesus.
